rd-school-c7-maths.ch06-triangle-propert.title: The Triangle and its Properties
rd-school-c7-maths.ch06-triangle-propert.subtitle: Medians, altitudes, the 180° rule, the exterior-angle shortcut, the triangle inequality and Pythagoras.

sections.md:
Look at the Howrah Bridge, a mobile tower, or the roof of a railway platform: triangles everywhere. Push on a square frame of sticks and it squashes into a rhombus. Push on a triangle and it **refuses to change shape**. That rigidity comes from the properties in this chapter.

**Recall.** A triangle is a closed figure made of three line segments. △ABC has
- three **sides**: AB, BC, CA;
- three **angles**: ∠A, ∠B, ∠C;
- three **vertices**: A, B, C.
The side opposite vertex A is BC; the angle opposite side AB is ∠C.

**Classifying triangles**

| By sides | By angles |
|---|---|
| **Scalene** — all sides different | **Acute** — all angles < 90° |
| **Isosceles** — two sides equal | **Right** — one angle = 90° |
| **Equilateral** — all sides equal | **Obtuse** — one angle > 90° |

A triangle can be, for example, both isosceles and right (angles 45°, 45°, 90°).

check.q: A triangle with sides 7 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm is—
check.why: Exactly two sides are equal (7 cm each), which is the definition of an isosceles triangle.

sections.md:
A **median** connects a vertex to the **mid-point of the opposite side**.

- Every triangle has **3 medians**, one from each vertex.
- The three medians always meet at **one point** called the **centroid**. (You'll study it in later classes; it is the triangle's balancing point — cut a triangle from cardboard and it balances on a pencil tip placed at the centroid!)
- Medians always lie **inside** the triangle, whatever its shape.

**Paper-folding activity.** Cut out a triangle. Fold it so that B falls on C; the crease marks the mid-point of BC. Now fold through A and that mid-point — that crease is a median.

check.q: How many medians does a triangle have?
check.why: One median can be drawn from each of the three vertices to the mid-point of the opposite side.

sections.md:
An **altitude** is the **perpendicular** line segment from a vertex to the opposite side (or to the line containing it). It gives the **height** of the triangle.

- Every triangle has **3 altitudes**.
- In an **acute** triangle, all altitudes lie **inside**.
- In a **right** triangle, two altitudes are the **legs themselves** (the sides forming the right angle).
- In an **obtuse** triangle, two altitudes fall **outside** — you must extend the opposite sides to draw them.

**Median vs altitude**

| Median | Altitude |
|---|---|
| Goes to the mid-point | Meets the side at 90° |
| Always inside | Can be outside (obtuse) |
| Meet at centroid | Meet at orthocentre |

In an **isosceles** triangle, the median and altitude from the vertex between the equal sides are the **same line**. In an **equilateral** triangle, this is true from every vertex.

check.q: In an obtuse-angled triangle, how many altitudes lie outside the triangle?
check.why: The two altitudes from the acute-angle vertices fall on the extensions of the opposite sides, outside the triangle; only one is inside.

sections.md:
Extend side BC of △ABC beyond C to a point D. The angle ∠ACD formed outside is an **exterior angle**. The two angles of the triangle not next to it, ∠A and ∠B, are its **interior opposite angles**.

> **Exterior angle property:** An exterior angle equals the **sum of its two interior opposite angles**: ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B.

**Why?** ∠ACD and ∠ACB form a linear pair, so ∠ACD = 180° − ∠C. By the angle-sum property (next section) ∠A + ∠B = 180° − ∠C. So both equal 180° − ∠C. ✔

**Activity.** Cut out copies of ∠A and ∠B and place them side by side at C next to the extended line — they exactly fill ∠ACD.

**Examples**
- Interior opposite angles 50° and 60° → exterior angle **110°**.
- Exterior angle 120°, one interior opposite angle 45° → the other is **75°**.

An exterior angle is always **greater than each** interior opposite angle. At each vertex there are two exterior angles (extend either side), and they are equal as vertically opposite angles.

check.q: An exterior angle of a triangle is 105° and one interior opposite angle is 40°. The other interior opposite angle is—
check.why: The exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles, so the other angle is 105° − 40° = 65°.

sections.md:
> **The three angles of every triangle add up to 180°.**

**Activity 1 — tear the corners.** Draw any triangle, tear off its three corners, and place them side by side with vertices touching. They form a **straight line** — 180°.

**Activity 2 — paper folding.** Fold a triangle so the vertex A touches the base; then fold B and C to the same point. The three angles fit along a straight edge.

**Proof using parallel lines.** Through A, draw line PQ ∥ BC. Then ∠PAB = ∠B and ∠QAC = ∠C (alternate angles). And ∠PAB + ∠A + ∠QAC = 180° (straight line). So ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°.

**Consequences**
- A triangle can have **at most one right angle** or **one obtuse angle**.
- In a right triangle, the two acute angles are **complementary**.
- Each angle of an equilateral triangle = 180° ÷ 3 = **60°**.

**Examples**
- Two angles are 30° and 80° → third = 180° − 110° = **70°**.
- Angles in ratio 2 : 3 : 4 → 2x + 3x + 4x = 180 → x = 20 → **40°, 60°, 80°**.

check.q: Can a triangle have angles 95°, 60° and 35°?
check.why: 95° + 60° + 35° = 190°, not 180°, so these cannot be the angles of a triangle.

sections.h: Two special triangles: equilateral and isosceles
sections.md:
**Equilateral triangle**
- All three sides equal.
- All three angles equal, each **60°**.
- Fold it along any median: the halves match exactly — it has **3 lines of symmetry**.

**Isosceles triangle**
- Two sides equal; the third side is the **base**.
- The angles **opposite the equal sides are equal** (the base angles).
- Fold it so the equal sides overlap: the base angles match. It has **1 line of symmetry**.
- Converse: if two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite them are equal.

**Examples**
- Isosceles with vertex angle 40° → base angles (180 − 40)/2 = **70° each**.
- Isosceles with a base angle 50° → vertex angle = 180 − 100 = **80°**.
- In △PQR, ∠P = ∠Q = 65°. Then PR = QR, and ∠R = 50°.

check.q: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 100°. Each base angle is—
check.why: The base angles are equal and together make 180° − 100° = 80°, so each is 40°.

sections.h: Sum of the lengths of two sides — the triangle inequality
sections.md:
Can you make a triangle from sticks of 3 cm, 4 cm and 10 cm? Try it: the 3 cm and 4 cm sticks lie flat and can't reach across 10 cm.

> **The sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle is greater than the third side.**

Also, the **difference** of any two sides is **less than** the third side.

**Why?** The straight path between two points is the shortest. Going from B to C directly (side BC) is shorter than going B → A → C (AB + AC).

**Testing** whether 3 lengths can form a triangle: check that the **two smaller** add to more than the **largest**.
- 2, 3, 5: 2 + 3 = 5, not greater → **No**.
- 6, 3, 2: 3 + 2 = 5 < 6 → **No**.
- 10.2, 5.8, 4.5: 5.8 + 4.5 = 10.3 > 10.2 → **Yes**.

**Range of the third side.** Two sides are 12 cm and 15 cm. The third side must be more than 15 − 12 = 3 and less than 15 + 12 = 27: between **3 cm and 27 cm**.

check.q: Which lengths can form a triangle?
check.why: For 4, 5, 8 the two smaller sides sum to 9, which is greater than 8; the others fail this test.

sections.h: Right-angled triangles and the Pythagoras property
sections.md:
In a right triangle, the side opposite the right angle is the **hypotenuse** — the longest side. The other two are the **legs**.

> **Pythagoras property:** In a right triangle, (hypotenuse)² = (leg)² + (leg)².

**See it.** Draw a right triangle with legs 3 cm and 4 cm; measure the hypotenuse: 5 cm. Squares: 9 + 16 = 25 = 5² ✔. Build squares on each side with graph paper — the two small squares' areas together equal the big one.

**Converse:** if the square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is **right-angled**, with the right angle opposite that longest side.
- 6, 8, 10: 36 + 64 = 100 → right triangle.
- 2, 2, 3: 4 + 4 = 8 ≠ 9 → not right.

**Pythagorean triples**: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), and multiples like (6, 8, 10).

**Real problem.** A 15 m ladder reaches a window 12 m high. How far is its foot from the wall? 15² = 12² + d² → 225 = 144 + d² → d² = 81 → **d = 9 m**.

**Did you know?** The Baudhayana Shulba Sutra (composed many centuries BCE — historians date it roughly to 800–500 BCE) states this relationship for the diagonal of a rectangle, used in building fire-altars. The property is named after the Greek Pythagoras, but it was known in India, Babylon and China too.

check.q: The legs of a right triangle are 5 cm and 12 cm. The hypotenuse is—
check.why: Hypotenuse² = 25 + 144 = 169, and √169 = 13 cm.

workedExamples.q: Find x if the angles of a triangle are x, 2x and 3x.
An exterior angle is 130° and the interior opposite angles are equal. Find them.
A tree breaks 5 m above the ground and its top touches the ground 12 m from the base. Find the original height.
steps: Broken part is the hypotenuse: h² = 5² + 12² = 169 → h = 13 m.

workedExamples.q: Is it possible to have a triangle with sides 6 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm?
A rectangle has sides 40 cm and 30 cm. Find its diagonal.
steps: Diagonal splits it into right triangles: d² = 40² + 30² = 1600 + 900 = 2500.

workedExamples.q: In a right triangle one acute angle is 35°. Find the other.
steps: The acute angles of a right triangle are complementary.

summary: A triangle has 3 sides, 3 angles and 3 vertices; classify by sides and by angles.
A median joins a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side; the 3 medians meet at the centroid.
An altitude is perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side; it may lie outside in an obtuse triangle.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
The angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite equal sides are equal.
Sum of any two sides > third side; difference of any two sides < third side.
Hypotenuse² = leg² + leg² in a right triangle (Pythagoras property), and the converse holds.

glossary.d: Segment from a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side
Perpendicular segment from a vertex to the opposite side
Angle formed by one side and the extension of an adjacent side
Side opposite the right angle; the longest side

rd-school-c7-maths.ch06-triangle-propert.title: The Triangle and its Properties (part 2)
rd-school-c7-maths.ch06-triangle-propert.subtitle: Cut-and-tear activities, the converse of Pythagoras, and every exercise type solved.

sections.h: Activities: see the properties with your own hands
sections.md:
**Tear-the-corners (angle sum).** Draw any triangle on paper, colour its three corners, and tear them off. Place the three torn corners side by side with their tips touching at one point. They fit exactly along a straight line — 180°. Try it with a thin obtuse triangle and a fat acute one: always a straight line.

**Fold-the-corners (angle sum again).** Cut out a triangle. Fold the top vertex down so it touches the base along the altitude. Fold the two other corners in so they meet the first one. The three angles now sit together on the base line — again 180°.

**Exterior-angle cut-out.** Draw △ABC and extend BC to D, making the exterior angle ∠ACD. Cut copies of ∠A and ∠B and place them side by side inside ∠ACD. They cover it exactly: **exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles**.

**Straws and sticks (triangle inequality).** Take sticks of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm. Try to make a triangle — the two short ones cannot reach each other because 3 + 4 = 7 is less than 8. With 5 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm it works (5 + 6 = 11 > 8).

**Squares on sides (Pythagoras).** On squared paper draw a right triangle with legs 3 and 4 units. Build squares on all three sides. Count: 9 + 16 = 25 unit squares, and the square on the hypotenuse has 25.

check.q: When the three torn corners of a triangle are placed together, they form—
check.why: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°, which is a straight angle.

sections.h: Pythagoras in reverse, and the range of the third side
sections.md:
**Converse of the Pythagoras property.** If in a triangle the square of one side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle **is right-angled**, and the right angle is opposite the longest side.

- Sides 6, 8, 10: 36 + 64 = 100 = 10² → right-angled.
- Sides 5, 12, 13: 25 + 144 = 169 → right-angled.
- Sides 4, 5, 6: 16 + 25 = 41 ≠ 36 → **not** right-angled.

Always test with the **longest** side as the possible hypotenuse.

**Range of the third side.** If two sides are 12 cm and 15 cm, the third side x must satisfy
- x < 12 + 15 = 27, and
- x > 15 − 12 = 3.
So 3 cm < x < 27 cm. The rule: the third side lies **between the difference and the sum** of the other two.

**Real life.** A 15 m ladder leans on a wall with its foot 9 m away. Height reached = √(15² − 9²) = √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12 m. A tree broken by a storm, a TV screen's diagonal, a cricket pitch corner-to-corner — all Pythagoras problems.

**Did you know?** Baudhayana's Sulba Sutra (an ancient Indian text on building altars) states this relation between the sides of a rectangle and its diagonal, centuries before it was popularly credited to Pythagoras.

check.q: Which set of sides forms a right triangle?
check.why: 49 + 576 = 625 = 25², so by the converse of Pythagoras the triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 is right-angled.

sections.h: Exercise types and how to attack them
sections.md:
| Type | Key idea |
|---|---|
| Identify median / altitude in a figure | median → mid-point; altitude → perpendicular |
| Find an exterior angle or interior opposite angle | exterior = sum of interior opposite |
| Find unknown angles x, y | angle sum 180°, plus linear pair |
| Equal angles in isosceles/equilateral triangles | base angles equal; equilateral 60° each |
| Can these lengths make a triangle? | sum of any two sides > third |
| Range of the third side | difference < x < sum |
| Find a side in a right triangle | hypotenuse² = leg² + leg² |
| Is it right-angled? | converse of Pythagoras |

**Two-step example.** In △PQR, ∠P = 2x, ∠Q = 3x and the exterior angle at R is 120°. Exterior angle = ∠P + ∠Q → 5x = 120 → x = 24. So ∠P = 48°, ∠Q = 72°, and ∠R = 180 − 120 = 60°. Check: 48 + 72 + 60 = 180 ✔.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch07-comparing-quanti.title: Comparing Quantities
rd-school-c7-maths.ch07-comparing-quanti.subtitle: Ratios, percentages, profit and loss, and simple interest — the maths of every shop, bank and cricket stat.

sections.md:
Anika scored 18 out of 25 in Science. Bhavya scored 32 out of 40 in Maths. Who did better? You can't compare 18 and 32 directly — the totals differ. We need a **common way to compare**: ratios and percentages.

**Ratio recap.** A ratio a : b compares two quantities of the **same kind in the same unit**. It is written in lowest terms.
- 30 minutes to 2 hours → 30 min : 120 min = **1 : 4** (convert units first!)
- 2 m to 50 cm → 200 cm : 50 cm = **4 : 1**

**Equivalent ratios.** Multiply or divide both terms by the same number: 1 : 2 = 2 : 4 = 5 : 10.

**Comparing ratios.** Is 3 : 4 bigger than 2 : 3? Write as fractions 3/4 and 2/3, use a common denominator: 9/12 vs 8/12 → **3 : 4 is greater**.

**Example — recipe.** A tea recipe uses milk and water in ratio 2 : 3. For 15 cups of water, milk = 2/3 × 15 = **10 cups**.

**Proportion.** When two ratios are equal, the four numbers are **in proportion**: 2 : 3 :: 10 : 15. (Extremes product 2 × 15 = means product 3 × 10.)

check.q: The ratio of 50 paise to ₹2 is—
check.why: Convert to the same unit: ₹2 = 200 paise, so 50 : 200 = 1 : 4.

sections.md:
**Per cent** comes from Latin *per centum*, 'for each hundred'. Symbol: **%**. So 35% = 35/100.

**When the total is 100**, the percentage is just the count. 100 beads: 40 red → 40% red.

**When the total isn't 100**, scale it:
> Percentage = (part ÷ whole) × 100%

Back to the puzzle:
- Anika: 18/25 × 100 = **72%**
- Bhavya: 32/40 × 100 = **80%** → Bhavya did better.

**Fractions to percent** — multiply by 100%:
- 1/2 = 50%, 1/4 = 25%, 3/4 = 75%, 1/5 = 20%, 1/3 = 33⅓%, 1/8 = 12.5%

**Decimals to percent** — multiply by 100 (shift the point two places right):
- 0.75 = 75%, 0.09 = 9%, 0.2 = 20%, 1.25 = 125%

**Percent to fraction or decimal** — divide by 100:
- 45% = 45/100 = 9/20 = 0.45; 5% = 1/20 = 0.05; 150% = 1.5

**Fun with estimation.** Shade about 25% of a figure; estimate what percent of a glass is filled. Percentages also add up to 100% for the parts of a whole: if 65% of a class is girls, 35% are boys.

sections.h: Using percentages — 'how many?' and ratios to percent
sections.md:
**Finding a percentage of a quantity** — multiply by the percent as a fraction.
- 25% of 360 students = 25/100 × 360 = **90**.
- 8% of ₹2500 = **₹200**.
- 12% of 250 litres = **30 litres**.

**Finding the whole from a part.** 9 is 25% of what number? 25/100 × x = 9 → x = **36**.

**Interpreting percentages.** '25% of people in a town own a car' means 25 out of every 100. In a town of 40 000, that's 10 000 car owners.

**Ratios to percentages.** Divide ₹1200 among A, B, C in ratio 1 : 2 : 3. Total parts 6.
- A = 1/6 = 16⅔%, B = 2/6 = 33⅓%, C = 3/6 = 50% (they add to 100%).
- Money: A ₹200, B ₹400, C ₹600.

**Example — soil.** Soil has 30% clay and 70% sand... If a field sample of 5 kg is analysed, clay = 1.5 kg.

**Example — votes.** In an election of 5000 votes, a candidate gets 54%. Votes = **2700**. Her rival with the rest gets 2300 (46%).

check.q: What is 15% of 80?

sections.h: Increase or decrease as a percent
sections.md:
Prices rise, populations grow, a phone's battery drops. To compare such changes we use **percentage change**.

> Percentage increase = (Increase ÷ Original amount) × 100%
> Percentage decrease = (Decrease ÷ Original amount) × 100%

Always divide by the **original** (old) value!

**Examples**
- School fee rose from ₹4000 to ₹4500. Increase = 500. % increase = 500/4000 × 100 = **12.5%**.
- A shirt was ₹800; now ₹680. Decrease = 120. % decrease = 120/800 × 100 = **15%**.
- A town of 25 000 grows by 8%. New population = 25 000 + 2000 = **27 000**.
- The price of a scooter is ₹68 000 and falls by 20%. New price = 80% of 68 000 = **₹54 400**.

**Trap!** A price up 10% then down 10% does **not** return to the start. ₹100 → ₹110 → ₹99.

check.q: A book's price rose from ₹200 to ₹250. The percentage increase is—
check.why: Increase = 50; divide by the original 200 and multiply by 100 to get 25%.

sections.h: Prices related to buying and selling — profit and loss
sections.md:
**Cost price (CP)** — the price at which an item is bought. **Selling price (SP)** — the price at which it is sold.

- If SP > CP → **Profit** = SP − CP
- If CP > SP → **Loss** = CP − SP
- If SP = CP → neither profit nor loss.

**Overhead expenses** (transport, repairs, packing) are **added to CP**. A bicycle bought for ₹3000 with ₹200 spent on repairs has CP = ₹3200.

**Profit or loss as a percentage** — always **on CP**:
> Profit% = (Profit ÷ CP) × 100; Loss% = (Loss ÷ CP) × 100

**Examples**
- Bought a mobile cover for ₹150, sold for ₹180. Profit = 30. Profit% = 30/150 × 100 = **20%**.
- Bought a chair for ₹1200, sold for ₹960. Loss = 240. Loss% = 240/1200 × 100 = **20%**.
- CP ₹500, profit 12%. SP = 500 + 12% of 500 = 500 + 60 = **₹560**.
- SP ₹1080 after a 10% loss. 90% of CP = 1080 → CP = **₹1200**.
- Juhi sells a washing machine for ₹13 500 and loses 20%. CP = 13 500 ÷ 0.8 = **₹16 875**.

**Two items, overall result.** A shopkeeper buys two bulbs at ₹10 each, sells one at 10% profit and the other at 10% loss. SP = 11 + 9 = 20 = CP → **no overall profit or loss**.

check.q: A toy bought for ₹240 is sold for ₹300. The profit percent is—
check.why: Profit = 60 and profit% is calculated on CP: 60/240 × 100 = 25%.

sections.h: Charge given on borrowed money — simple interest
sections.md:
When you borrow money from a bank (or deposit money in it), there is an extra charge called **interest**.

- **Principal (P)** — the money borrowed or deposited.
- **Rate (R)** — interest per ₹100 per year, e.g. 8% per annum (p.a.).
- **Time (T)** — in years.
- **Amount (A)** — total paid back = Principal + Interest.

> **Simple interest SI = (P × R × T) ÷ 100**, and A = P + SI.

**Examples**
- ₹10 000 at 15% p.a. for 1 year: SI = 10 000 × 15 × 1 / 100 = **₹1500**; A = **₹11 500**.
- ₹56 000 at 10% for 2 years: SI = 56 000 × 10 × 2 / 100 = **₹11 200**; A = ₹67 200.
- ₹2400 at 5% for 3 years: SI = **₹360**.
- Time in months: ₹6000 at 9% for 8 months: T = 8/12 years → SI = 6000 × 9 × 8 / 1200 = **₹360**.

**Finding the unknown**
- What rate gives ₹280 interest on ₹2000 in 2 years? 280 = 2000 × R × 2 / 100 → R = **7%**.
- How long for ₹1500 at 8% to earn ₹480? 480 = 1500 × 8 × T / 100 → T = **4 years**.
- Principal earning ₹900 at 6% in 3 years? 900 = P × 18/100 → P = **₹5000**.

**Did you know?** This chapter's simple interest stays the same every year. Banks often use **compound interest**, where interest earns interest — you'll meet it in Class 8. (For real savings decisions, check with your bank or a SEBI-registered adviser.)

rd-school-c7-maths.ch07-comparing-quanti.title: Comparing Quantities (part 2)
rd-school-c7-maths.ch07-comparing-quanti.subtitle: Converting fractions, decimals and percents, profit with overheads, and interest worked backwards.

sections.h: Fractions, decimals and percentages — three faces of one number
sections.md:
A shopkeeper's banner says '25% off', the newspaper says 'one-quarter of voters', and a cricket stat says 'strike rate 0.25 per ball'. All three mean the same amount.

**Fraction → percent:** multiply by 100%. 3/5 = 3/5 × 100% = 60%. 7/8 = 87.5%.
**Decimal → percent:** move the decimal point two places right. 0.45 = 45%; 1.2 = 120%; 0.075 = 7.5%.
**Percent → fraction:** put over 100 and simplify. 35% = 35/100 = 7/20.
**Percent → decimal:** divide by 100. 8% = 0.08.

| Fraction | Decimal | Percent |
|---|---|---|
| 1/2 | 0.5 | 50% |
| 1/4 | 0.25 | 25% |
| 1/5 | 0.2 | 20% |
| 1/8 | 0.125 | 12.5% |
| 3/4 | 0.75 | 75% |

**Parts of a whole.** If 72% of a class of 25 students like cricket, 28% don't. Number who like cricket = 72/100 × 25 = 18; others = 7. Percentages of all the parts always add to 100%.

**Estimating.** 'About what percent of this circle is shaded?' — if one-third is shaded, it is about 33⅓%.

check.q: 0.06 written as a percent is—
check.why: To change a decimal to a percent multiply by 100, and 0.06 × 100 = 6, so it is 6%.

sections.h: Profit and loss as a percentage, with overhead expenses
sections.md:
Profit % and loss % are always calculated **on the cost price (CP)**:
- Profit % = (Profit ÷ CP) × 100
- Loss % = (Loss ÷ CP) × 100

**Overhead expenses.** If Ravi buys an old scooter for ₹12,000 and spends ₹3,000 on repairs, his real CP = ₹15,000. Selling at ₹18,000 gives profit ₹3,000 → 3000/15000 × 100 = **20%**.

**Working backwards.**
- *SP from CP and profit %*: CP ₹500, profit 12% → SP = 500 + 60 = ₹560.
- *CP from SP and loss %*: sold at ₹720 with loss 10% → SP is 90% of CP → CP = 720 × 100/90 = ₹800.

**Mixed deals.** A trader buys two fans at ₹1,000 each, sells one at 20% profit (₹1,200) and the other at 10% loss (₹900). Total CP ₹2,000, total SP ₹2,100 → overall profit ₹100 = 5%.

check.q: CP = ₹400, SP = ₹340. Loss % is—
check.why: Loss = ₹60 and loss % = 60/400 × 100 = 15%, always calculated on the cost price.

sections.h: Simple interest: more years, and finding rate or time
sections.md:
SI = (P × R × T) ÷ 100, and **Amount A = P + SI**.

**Interest for several years.** ₹10,000 at 5% per year: interest is ₹500 every year, so after 3 years SI = ₹1,500 and A = ₹11,500.

**Finding the rate.** ₹2,400 earns ₹288 in 2 years: R = (SI × 100) ÷ (P × T) = 28,800 ÷ 4,800 = **6%** per year.

**Finding the time.** ₹5,000 at 8% earns ₹1,200: T = (1200 × 100) ÷ (5000 × 8) = 120,000 ÷ 40,000 = **3 years**.

**Finding the principal.** Interest ₹450 in 3 years at 5%: P = (450 × 100) ÷ (5 × 3) = ₹3,000.

**Months.** Convert to years: 9 months = 9/12 = ¾ year.

**Did you know?** Banks and post-office schemes in India mostly use *compound* interest, which you'll learn in Class 8; simple interest is the starting point. For real savings decisions, ask your bank.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch08-rational-numbers.title: Rational Numbers
rd-school-c7-maths.ch08-rational-numbers.subtitle: Fractions that can be negative: standard form, the number line, comparing, and all four operations.

sections.md:
A diver is 3/4 km… no, let's be realistic: a diver is **¾ m below** a diving board's base level, and a kite is 5/2 m above it. With integers alone we can say '2 m below' but not '¾ m below'. With fractions alone we can say '¾' but not 'below'. We need numbers that are **both** fractional and possibly negative.

Our number family has grown step by step:
- **Natural numbers** 1, 2, 3, … — for counting.
- **Whole numbers** 0, 1, 2, … — add zero.
- **Integers** …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … — add negatives (so 3 − 5 has an answer).
- **Fractions** — so 3 ÷ 4 has an answer.
- **Rational numbers** — combine the two ideas, so (−3) ÷ 4 has an answer.

If 1 km above sea level is +1 km, then 3/4 km below is **−3/4 km**. A loss of ₹3/2 lakh is **−3/2**.

check.q: Which number system first lets 5 − 8 have an answer?
check.why: 5 − 8 = −3, a negative number, and integers are the first set to include negatives.

sections.md:
The word *rational* comes from **ratio**.

> A **rational number** is a number that can be written as **p/q**, where p and q are **integers** and **q ≠ 0**.

Examples: 2/3, −5/7, 7/(−9), −12/−5, 0/4.

- Every **integer** is rational: −6 = −6/1, 0 = 0/1.
- Every **fraction** is rational: 3/8.
- Every terminating decimal is rational: 0.5 = 1/2, −1.25 = −5/4.

**Numerator and denominator** — in −5/7, numerator −5, denominator 7.

**Equivalent rational numbers.** Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer:
> −2/3 = −4/6 = −6/9 = 10/(−15)

To check whether −3/5 and 9/(−15) are equivalent: 9/(−15) = (9 ÷ −3)/(−15 ÷ −3) = −3/5 ✔.

**Positive and negative rationals**
- **Positive** if numerator and denominator have the **same sign**: 2/3, −5/−8.
- **Negative** if they have **opposite signs**: −2/3, 5/(−8).
- **0 is neither** positive nor negative.

check.q: Which of these is a negative rational number?
check.why: In 5/(−11) the numerator and denominator have opposite signs, so the number is negative.

sections.h: Rational numbers on a number line
sections.md:
Mark 0 in the middle, positive numbers to the right and negative to the left — just like integers. To place a rational number, **divide each unit into as many equal parts as the denominator**.

- To mark 3/4: split 0–1 into 4 parts, take 3 parts to the right.
- To mark −3/4: take 3 parts to the **left** of 0.
- To mark 7/4 = 1¾: go past 1 by 3 more quarters.
- −5/2 = −2½: halfway between −2 and −3.

Numbers **equally far** from 0 on opposite sides are **opposites** (additive inverses): 3/4 and −3/4.

sections.md:
A rational number is in **standard form** when
1. its **denominator is a positive** integer, and
2. numerator and denominator have **no common factor other than 1**.

**Steps to reduce:**
- Move any negative sign to the numerator: 5/(−8) = −5/8.
- Divide numerator and denominator by their HCF (ignoring signs).

**Examples**
- −18/45 → HCF 9 → **−2/5**
- 36/(−24) → −36/24 → HCF 12 → **−3/2**
- −44/−72 → 44/72 → HCF 4 → **11/18**
- 0/−7 → **0**

check.q: The standard form of 24/(−36) is—
check.why: Move the sign up to get −24/36, then divide by the HCF 12 to get −2/3 with a positive denominator.

sections.md:
**Rules**
- Every **positive** rational is greater than 0, and 0 is greater than every **negative** rational.
- A positive rational is always greater than a negative one: 1/100 > −50.
- For two **negatives**, compare as if positive and then **reverse**: since 2/5 < 3/5, we get −2/5 **>** −3/5. (On the number line −2/5 is closer to 0, further right.)

**Method for any two:** write both in standard form with the **same positive denominator** (use the LCM), then compare numerators.

- Compare −2/3 and −4/5: LCM 15 → −10/15 and −12/15. Since −10 > −12, **−2/3 > −4/5**.
- Compare 5/(−6) and −7/9: → −5/6 vs −7/9 → −15/18 vs −14/18 → **−7/9 is greater**.

**Rational numbers between two rationals.** Between two integers like 1 and 2 there is no integer. But between any two rational numbers there are **infinitely many** rationals!

- Between −2/5 and 1/2: write as −4/10 and 5/10 → −3/10, −2/10, −1/10, 0, 1/10, … — and you can always use bigger denominators to get more.
- **Mean method:** halfway between a and b is (a + b)/2. Between 1/4 and 1/2: (1/4 + 1/2)/2 = 3/8. Repeat to get as many as you want.

check.q: Which is greater: −3/4 or −5/6?
check.why: With denominator 12 they are −9/12 and −10/12; −9 is greater than −10, so −3/4 is greater.

sections.md:
**Same denominators** — add numerators, keep the denominator.
- 7/3 + (−5)/3 = (7 − 5)/3 = **2/3**
- −6/5 + (−2)/5 = **−8/5**

**Different denominators** — use the LCM.
- −7/5 + (−2)/3: LCM 15 → −21/15 + (−10)/15 = **−31/15**
- −2/3 + 3/4 → −8/12 + 9/12 = **1/12**

**Additive inverse.** −4/7 + 4/7 = 0, so they are additive inverses. The additive inverse of a/b is −a/b.

**Subtraction** — add the additive inverse.
> a/b − c/d = a/b + (additive inverse of c/d)
- 5/7 − 3/8 = 40/56 − 21/56 = **19/56**
- 2/3 − (−4/5) = 2/3 + 4/5 = 10/15 + 12/15 = **22/15** = 1 7/15
- Mixed numbers: −2⅓ − 1½ = −7/3 − 3/2 = −14/6 − 9/6 = **−23/6**

check.why: With denominator 12, −9/12 + 10/12 = 1/12.

sections.md:
**Multiplication** — multiply numerators and denominators, then reduce.
> (a/b) × (c/d) = (a × c)/(b × d)
- (−3/5) × 2 = **−6/5**
- (−3/5) × (−2/7) = **6/35**
- (−9/2) × (5/4) = **−45/8**
- Sign rules are the same as for integers: same signs → positive; different → negative.

**On the number line**, (−3/5) × 2 means two jumps of 3/5 to the left → −6/5.

**Reciprocal (multiplicative inverse).** The reciprocal of a/b is **b/a** (a ≠ 0), since a/b × b/a = 1.
- Reciprocal of −8/9 is **−9/8** (the sign stays!).
- Reciprocal of −5 is −1/5. **0 has no reciprocal.**

**Division** — multiply by the reciprocal.
> a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c (c ≠ 0)
- (−7/2) ÷ (4/3) = −7/2 × 3/4 = **−21/8**
- (−6/5) ÷ (−3/10) = −6/5 × (−10/3) = 60/15 = **4**
- (3/13) ÷ (−4/65) = 3/13 × (−65/4) = **−15/4**

**Summary of results**: the sum, difference, product of two rationals is always rational; the quotient is rational as long as we don't divide by 0.

**Did you know?** Not every number is rational! The diagonal of a 1 m square is √2 m, and √2 cannot be written as p/q. Such numbers are called **irrational** — you'll meet them in Class 9.

check.why: Multiply by the reciprocal: −4/5 × 15/2 = −60/10 = −6.

summary: A rational number is p/q with p, q integers and q ≠ 0; integers and fractions are rational.
Multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer gives an equivalent rational number.
Same signs → positive; opposite signs → negative; 0 is neither.
On the number line, divide each unit into as many parts as the denominator.
Standard form: positive denominator and no common factor other than 1.
To compare, use a common positive denominator; for negatives, the one closer to 0 is greater.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch08-rational-numbers.title: Rational Numbers (part 2)
rd-school-c7-maths.ch08-rational-numbers.subtitle: Equivalent forms, positive vs negative, numbers hiding between numbers, inverses and reciprocals.

sections.md:
Multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator of a rational number by the **same non-zero integer** gives an **equivalent** rational number.

- −2/3 = −4/6 = −6/9 = −8/12 (multiply by 2, 3, 4)
- −10/15 = −2/3 (divide by 5)

**Finding a missing number.** −3/7 = ?/35 → 35 ÷ 7 = 5, so ? = −3 × 5 = −15. And 4/−9 = −16/? → (−16) ÷ 4 = −4, so ? = −9 × (−4) = 36.

**Test for equality (cross-multiply).** a/b = c/d when a × d = b × c. Is −4/6 = 6/−9? (−4)(−9) = 36 and 6 × 6 = 36 → yes.

A chapati cut into 2 with you eating 1 piece, or cut into 4 with you eating 2 — you ate the same amount. Equivalent rationals are the same number in different clothes.

check.q: Which is equivalent to −5/8?
check.why: Multiplying numerator and denominator of −5/8 by 2 gives −10/16, an equivalent rational number.

sections.md:
- A rational number is **positive** when numerator and denominator have the **same sign**: 3/5, −2/−7 (= 2/7).
- It is **negative** when they have **opposite signs**: −3/5, 4/−9.
- **0 is neither** positive nor negative.

So −3/−5 is positive and 7/−2 is negative. Always move the minus sign to the numerator when writing in standard form: 7/−2 = −7/2.

**Did you know?** A temperature of −3.5 °C in Leh, a bank balance of −₹250 and a submarine at −12/5 km are all negative rational numbers in daily life.

check.q: Which of these is positive?
check.why: In −7/−3 both numerator and denominator are negative, so they have the same sign and the number is positive (7/3).

sections.h: Rational numbers between two rational numbers
sections.md:
Between 1 and 2 there is **no** integer — but there are **infinitely many** rational numbers.

**Method 1 — equivalent forms.** Find rationals between −2/5 and 1/2. Use the common denominator 10: −4/10 and 5/10. Between them: −3/10, −2/10, −1/10, 0, 1/10, 2/10, 3/10, 4/10. Need more? Use denominator 100: −40/100 to 50/100 gives 89 numbers in between.

**Method 2 — the mean.** (a + b)/2 always lies between a and b. Between 1/4 and 1/2: (1/4 + 1/2)/2 = (3/4)/2 = 3/8. Then between 1/4 and 3/8: 5/16. You can keep going forever.

This is a big difference from integers: rational numbers are **dense** — no gaps can be found between any two of them that don't contain more rationals.

check.q: Which rational number lies between −1/3 and 1/3?
check.why: 0 is greater than −1/3 and less than 1/3, so it lies between them.

sections.h: Additive inverse, reciprocal, and exercise types
sections.md:
**Additive inverse (negative).** The additive inverse of a/b is −a/b, because a/b + (−a/b) = 0. Inverse of 3/7 is −3/7; of −5/9 is 5/9.

Subtraction uses it: a/b − c/d = a/b + (additive inverse of c/d). Example: 5/6 − (−1/3) = 5/6 + 1/3 = 5/6 + 2/6 = 7/6.

**Reciprocal (multiplicative inverse).** The reciprocal of a/b (a ≠ 0) is b/a, because their product is 1. Reciprocal of −3/8 is −8/3. 0 has no reciprocal.

Division uses it: a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c. Example: −4/5 ÷ 2/15 = −4/5 × 15/2 = −60/10 = −6.

**Exercise types in this chapter:** list rationals between two given numbers; write next terms of patterns like −1/3, −2/6, −3/9…; draw on a number line; decide positive/negative; write equivalent forms and find missing terms; reduce to standard form; compare with <, >, =; arrange in ascending/descending order; add, subtract, multiply, divide; find additive inverse and reciprocal.

workedExamples.q: Write the next three terms: −1/4, −2/8, −3/12, …
steps: Numerator and denominator both change by the factor: −n/(4n).

summary: Multiplying/dividing numerator and denominator by the same non-zero integer gives an equivalent rational.
Same signs → positive; opposite signs → negative; 0 is neither.
Infinitely many rationals lie between any two rationals; the mean (a+b)/2 always works.
Additive inverse of a/b is −a/b; their sum is 0.
Reciprocal of a/b is b/a; their product is 1; 0 has no reciprocal.
Subtract by adding the additive inverse; divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch09-perimeter-area.title: Perimeter and Area
rd-school-c7-maths.ch09-perimeter-area.subtitle: Fencing, flooring and pizza: rectangles, parallelograms, triangles, circles, unit conversions and garden paths.

sections.h: Squares and rectangles — perimeter vs area
sections.md:
Ayaan's grandfather has a rectangular field 40 m by 25 m in Nashik. He wants to (a) put a wire fence around it and (b) spread fertiliser over it. Which needs **perimeter**, which needs **area**?

- **Perimeter** — the distance **around** a closed figure (fence, border, lace). Unit: m, cm.
- **Area** — the **surface** enclosed (fertiliser, tiles, paint). Unit: m², cm².

| Shape | Perimeter | Area |
|---|---|---|
| Rectangle (l, b) | 2(l + b) | l × b |
| Square (side a) | 4a | a × a = a² |

For the field: fence = 2(40 + 25) = **130 m**; area = 40 × 25 = **1000 m²**.

**Same area, different perimeters!** A 4 cm × 4 cm square and an 8 cm × 2 cm rectangle both have area 16 cm², but perimeters 16 cm and 20 cm. A square has the **least perimeter** for a given area among rectangles.

**Example.** A square plot has perimeter 64 m → side 16 m → area **256 m²**.

**Example — cost.** Tiling a floor 5 m × 4 m at ₹300 per m² costs 20 × 300 = **₹6000**. Skirting tiles around the walls at ₹50 per m: 18 m × 50 = **₹900**.

check.q: A rectangle is 12 cm long and has area 96 cm². Its perimeter is—
check.why: Breadth = 96 ÷ 12 = 8 cm, so perimeter = 2(12 + 8) = 40 cm.

sections.h: Triangles as parts of rectangles, and congruent parts
sections.md:
Cut a rectangle along a diagonal: you get **two congruent triangles**. So each triangle has **half** the area of the rectangle.

> Area of each right triangle = ½ × (length × breadth)

A 10 cm × 6 cm rectangle split by a diagonal gives two triangles of area **30 cm²** each.

**Square cut by both diagonals** → 4 congruent triangles, each ¼ of the square. A 5 cm square → each triangle 25/4 = 6.25 cm².

**Generalising.** If a figure is split into **congruent** parts, each part's area = total ÷ number of parts. But careful: two parts with **equal area need not be congruent** — a 6 × 2 rectangle and a 4 × 3 rectangle both have area 12 but different shapes.

**Activity.** Divide a square into 4 parts in different ways (strips, small squares, triangles) — each part is still ¼ of the area.

check.q: A square of side 8 cm is cut along both diagonals. What is the area of each triangle?
check.why: The square's area is 64 cm² and the diagonals make 4 congruent triangles, each 64 ÷ 4 = 16 cm².

sections.md:
**Activity.** Draw a parallelogram on paper. Drop a perpendicular from one top vertex to the base; cut off that right triangle and slide it to the other end. You get a **rectangle** with the same base and the same height!

> **Area of parallelogram = base × height** (b × h)

- **Base** — any side we choose.
- **Height (altitude)** — the **perpendicular** distance from the opposite side to that base. Not the slanted side!

A parallelogram can use **either pair** of sides as base, each with its own height. For ABCD with AB = 10 cm, height to AB = 6 cm, AD = 8 cm: area = 10 × 6 = 60 cm², so height to AD = 60 ÷ 8 = **7.5 cm**.

**Examples**
- b = 7 cm, h = 4 cm → **28 cm²**.
- Area 246 cm², base 20 cm → height **12.3 cm**.

fig.alt: Parallelogram with a triangle sliding across to form a rectangle

check.q: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and height 5 cm. Its area is—
check.why: Area of a parallelogram is base × height = 9 × 5 = 45 cm².

sections.md:
Take two **identical** triangles and fit them together — they always make a **parallelogram** with the same base and height. So

> **Area of triangle = ½ × base × height**

- The height is the perpendicular from the opposite vertex to the base (it may fall **outside** for an obtuse triangle — extend the base).
- All triangles on the same base and between the same parallels (same height) have **equal area**, however slanted.
- Any side can be the base, with its own height. In △ABC with BC = 12 cm and AD ⟂ BC = 5 cm, area = 30 cm². If AB = 13 cm, height from C to AB = 2 × 30 ÷ 13 ≈ 4.6 cm.

**Right triangle**: the two legs are base and height. Legs 6 cm and 8 cm → area **24 cm²**.

**Examples**
- b = 15 cm, h = 8 cm → **60 cm²**.
- Area 36 cm², base 9 cm → h = 2 × 36 ÷ 9 = **8 cm**.

check.q: A triangle has area 48 cm² and base 12 cm. Its height is—
check.why: From ½ × 12 × h = 48 we get 6h = 48, so h = 8 cm.

sections.md:
Wrap a thread around a bangle, then straighten it and measure. Divide by the bangle's diameter. Do it with a plate, a coin, a bucket lid — the answer is always a little more than 3. That magic constant is **π (pi)** ≈ **22/7** or **3.14**.

> **Circumference C = π × diameter = 2πr**

**Parts of a circle**: centre, radius (r), diameter (d = 2r), circumference (the perimeter of a circle).

**Examples**
- r = 7 cm → C = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = **44 cm**.
- d = 10 cm → C = 3.14 × 10 = **31.4 cm**.
- A wheel of radius 35 cm: one turn covers 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. In 1 km (100 000 cm) it turns 100 000 ÷ 220 ≈ **455 times**.
- Circumference 154 m → r = 154 ÷ (2 × 22/7) = **24.5 m**.

**Semicircle perimeter** = half the circumference + diameter = πr + 2r. For r = 7 cm: 22 + 14 = **36 cm**.

**Did you know?** Aryabhata (born 476 CE) gave a value of π equal to 3.1416, and described it as 'approximate' — a remarkable insight that π cannot be written exactly as a simple fraction.

check.q: The circumference of a circle with diameter 14 cm is (π = 22/7)—

sections.md:
**Activity.** Cut a paper circle into 16 equal sectors. Arrange them alternately up and down in a row. They form something very close to a **rectangle**:
- its length ≈ half the circumference = πr,
- its breadth ≈ the radius r.

> **Area of circle = πr × r = πr²**

**Examples**
- r = 7 cm → 22/7 × 49 = **154 cm²**.
- r = 14 cm → 22/7 × 196 = **616 cm²** (doubling r makes the area 4 times!).
- d = 10 m → r = 5 → 3.14 × 25 = **78.5 m²**.
- Circumference 44 cm → r = 7 → area **154 cm²**.

**Ring (annulus).** Area between circles of radii R and r = πR² − πr². A circular garden of radius 7 m with a 3.5 m wide path outside: R = 10.5 → π(110.25 − 49) = 22/7 × 61.25 = **192.5 m²**.

**Semicircle area** = ½πr².

check.q: The area of a circle of radius 21 cm is (π = 22/7)—

sections.md:
**Length**: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m.

**Area units square the conversion!**
- 1 cm² = 10 mm × 10 mm = **100 mm²**
- 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = **10 000 cm²**
- 1 hectare (ha) = 100 m × 100 m = **10 000 m²**
- 1 km² = 1000 m × 1000 m = **10 00 000 m²** (= 100 ha)

So 3 m² = 30 000 cm² (not 300!), and 50 000 m² = 5 ha.

**Applications — paths and borders**

**Path outside a rectangle.** A park is 30 m × 20 m with a 2.5 m path all around **outside**. Outer rectangle = 35 m × 25 m = 875 m². Park = 600 m². Path = **275 m²**.

**Path inside.** A 20 m × 15 m lawn has a 1.5 m border inside it. Inner = 17 × 12 = 204 m². Border = 300 − 204 = **96 m²**.

**Cross paths.** Two 3 m wide roads cross through the middle of a 90 m × 60 m park, parallel to the sides. Area = 90 × 3 + 60 × 3 − 3 × 3 = 270 + 180 − 9 = **441 m²** (subtract the overlap square, counted twice!).

**Picture frame.** A 20 cm × 15 cm photo in a frame 2 cm wide all round: outer 24 × 19 = 456; frame = 456 − 300 = **156 cm²**.

**Cost problems** — area × rate. Paving the cross roads above at ₹110 per m²: 441 × 110 = **₹48 510**.

check.q: How many cm² are there in 2 m²?
check.why: 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm², so 2 m² = 20 000 cm².

summary: Perimeter is the length of the boundary; area is the surface enclosed.
Rectangle: P = 2(l + b), A = l × b. Square: P = 4a, A = a².
A diagonal divides a rectangle into two congruent triangles of half its area.
Congruent parts have equal areas, but equal areas need not be congruent.
Parallelogram area = base × corresponding height.
Triangle area = ½ × base × height; two equal triangles make a parallelogram.
π ≈ 22/7 ≈ 3.14 is the ratio of circumference to diameter.
Circumference = 2πr = πd; area of circle = πr².
Area units square the length conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm², 1 ha = 10 000 m².
For paths: area of path = outer area − inner area; for cross roads, subtract the overlap once.

Perpendicular height to a chosen base

rd-school-c7-maths.ch09-perimeter-area-2.title: Perimeter and Area (part 2)
rd-school-c7-maths.ch09-perimeter-area-2.subtitle: Garden paths, crossroads in a park, and circular rings — the classic application problems.

sections.h: A path around (or inside) a rectangle
sections.md:
A school lawn is 30 m × 20 m. A path 2 m wide is built **outside** it, all around. What is the area of the path?

**Idea:** area of path = area of big outer rectangle − area of lawn.
- Outer length = 30 + 2 + 2 = 34 m; outer breadth = 20 + 2 + 2 = 24 m.
- Outer area = 34 × 24 = 816 m²; lawn area = 30 × 20 = 600 m².
- Path area = 816 − 600 = **216 m²**.
At ₹50 per m² for paving, cost = 216 × 50 = ₹10,800.

**Path inside.** If the 2 m path runs *inside* the boundary, the inner rectangle is (30 − 4) × (20 − 4) = 26 × 16 = 416 m², so path area = 600 − 416 = 184 m².

Remember: width is added (or subtracted) **on both sides**, so use 2 × width.

The same idea gives the area of a **border** on a saree, a **frame** around a photo, or the **margin** on a page.

check.q: A 10 m × 8 m room has a 1 m wide verandah outside all round. Verandah area?
check.why: Outer area is 12 × 10 = 120 m², room area is 80 m², so the verandah is 120 − 80 = 40 m².

sections.md:
A park 60 m × 40 m has two roads, each 3 m wide, running through the middle parallel to the sides, crossing like a plus sign.

- Road along the length: 60 × 3 = 180 m².
- Road along the breadth: 40 × 3 = 120 m².
- The central square where they cross (3 × 3 = 9 m²) has been **counted twice**, so subtract it once.
- Total road area = 180 + 120 − 9 = **291 m²**.
- Area of park left for grass = 2400 − 291 = 2109 m².

Forgetting the overlap is the most common mistake in this exercise type.

check.q: Why do we subtract the crossing square once?
options: It is not part of any road
It was counted in both roads
check.why: The central square belongs to both roads, so adding both road areas counts it twice, and one copy must be removed.

sections.h: Circular rings and other exercise types
sections.md:
**Ring (circular path).** A circular flower bed of radius 7 m has a 3.5 m wide path around it. Outer radius R = 10.5 m.
- Path area = πR² − πr² = 22/7 × (110.25 − 49) = 22/7 × 61.25 = **192.5 m²**.

**Wire bending.** A wire forms a square of side 11 cm (perimeter 44 cm). Bent into a circle: 2πr = 44 → r = 7 cm, area = 22/7 × 49 = 154 cm², more than the square's 121 cm². For a fixed perimeter, a circle encloses the most area.

**Wheel revolutions.** A wheel of radius 35 cm has circumference 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. To travel 1.1 km = 110,000 cm it turns 110,000 ÷ 220 = **500 times**.

**Exercise types:** perimeter/area of squares and rectangles; cost of fencing or tiling; area of triangles and parallelograms with base/height; finding an unknown side; circumference and area of circles; paths, borders and crossroads; unit conversion (1 m² = 10,000 cm²; 1 hectare = 10,000 m²).

workedExamples.q: A picture 40 cm × 30 cm has a 5 cm frame all round. Area of the frame?
How many times does a wheel of diameter 70 cm turn in covering 66 m?
A 1 m wide path runs inside a 20 m square plot. Path area?

summary: Area of a path = outer area − inner area.
A path of width w adds 2w to length and to breadth.
For crossroads, subtract the overlapping square once.
Area of a circular ring = π(R² − r²).
Distance covered in one revolution = circumference.
For a fixed perimeter, a circle has the greatest area.
1 hectare = 10,000 m².

rd-school-c7-maths.ch10-algebraic-expres.title: Algebraic Expressions
rd-school-c7-maths.ch10-algebraic-expres.subtitle: Terms, factors, coefficients, like terms, adding and subtracting, finding values, and writing rules and formulas.

sections.h: Matchstick patterns — how expressions are formed
sections.md:
Make a row of squares with matchsticks. 1 square needs 4 sticks, 2 squares need 7, 3 squares need 10… How many for 50 squares? Counting is slow. But notice: the first square takes 4, and each new one adds 3. For **n** squares: **3n + 1** sticks. For 50: 151. That little phrase **3n + 1** is an **algebraic expression**.

**Variables and constants**
- A **variable** can take different values: x, y, n, l.
- A **constant** has a fixed value: 4, −7, ½.

Expressions are formed by combining variables and constants with **+, −, ×, ÷**:
- x + 10 (10 added to x)
- 3y (y multiplied by 3)
- 2xy (x times y times 2)
- x² = x × x; 5xy² = 5 × x × y × y
- 4x − 5 (four times x, minus 5)
- p/3 + 2

**Writing expressions from words**
- 'Subtract z from y' → y − z
- 'One-half of the sum of x and y' → (x + y)/2
- 'The number 5 added to three times the product of m and n' → 3mn + 5
- 'Sum of the squares of p and q' → p² + q²
- 'Raju's father's age is 2 more than 3 times Raju's age (r)' → 3r + 2

check.q: The expression for '7 less than twice a number y' is—
check.why: Twice the number is 2y, and 7 less than that means subtracting 7, giving 2y − 7.

sections.md:
**Terms** are the parts of an expression joined by + or −. They are formed first, then added.

> In 4x + 5: terms are **4x** and **5**.
> In 4x² − 3xy: terms are **4x²** and **−3xy** (the sign belongs to the term).

**Factors** of a term are the numbers and variables multiplied to make it.
- 4x = 4 × x → factors 4 and x.
- −3xy = (−3) × x × y.
- 5x²y = 5 × x × x × y.

**Tree diagram.** For 4x² − 3xy, the expression branches into two terms, each branching into its factors (see the figure).

**Coefficient** — the **numerical factor** of a term.
- In 5xy, the coefficient is **5**.
- In −y, the coefficient is **−1**; in x², it is **1** (not written).
- Any factor can be called the coefficient of the rest: in 5xy, 5x is the coefficient of y. But usually 'coefficient' means the number part.

**Constant term** — a term with no variable (like 5 in 4x + 5).

check.q: What is the coefficient of x in −x + 5y?
check.why: −x means (−1) × x, so its numerical coefficient is −1.

sections.h: Like and unlike terms; monomials, binomials, trinomials
sections.md:
**Like terms** have the **same algebraic factors** (same variables with the same powers); only the numbers may differ.
- 2xy and −5xy → like.
- 7x² and 3x² → like.
- 4x and 4x² → **unlike** (different powers).
- 2xy and 2x → unlike.
- 3ab and 5ba → like (ab = ba).

**Naming expressions by the number of terms**

| Name | Terms | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Monomial | 1 | 7xy, −5m, 3z², 4 |
| Binomial | 2 | a + b, 4l + 5m, x² − 9 |
| Trinomial | 3 | x + y + 7, ab + a + b |
| Polynomial | 1 or more (whole-number powers of variables) | all of the above |

Careful: x + x + 3 looks like three terms but simplifies to 2x + 3 — a **binomial**. Always combine like terms before naming.

check.q: Which pair contains like terms?
check.why: 3x²y and −4yx² have exactly the same variable part x²y (order of multiplication doesn't matter), so they are like terms.

sections.h: Addition and subtraction of algebraic expressions
sections.md:
**Adding like terms** — add the coefficients, keep the variable part.
- 3x + 4x = 7x (3 pencils + 4 pencils = 7 pencils)
- 8xy − 3xy = 5xy
- 7x² + (−4x²) = 3x²

**Unlike terms cannot be combined**: 3x + 4y stays 3x + 4y (3 pencils + 4 erasers).

**Adding expressions**
- **Row method**: (3x + 5) + (4x − 2) = 3x + 4x + 5 − 2 = **7x + 3**.
- **Column method** — write like terms in the same column:

| | x² terms | x terms | constants |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7x² − 4x + 5 | 7x² | −4x | +5 |
| 16x − 9 | — | +16x | −9 |
| **Sum** | **7x²** | **+12x** | **−4** |

So the sum is **7x² + 12x − 4**.

**Subtracting expressions** — subtracting means adding the **additive inverse**: **change the sign of every term** being subtracted, then add.
- (5x² − 3xy + 4) − (2x² + xy − 7) = 5x² − 3xy + 4 − 2x² − xy + 7 = **3x² − 4xy + 11**.
- Subtract 4a − 7ab + 3b + 12 from 12a − 9ab + 5b − 3: 12a − 4a − 9ab + 7ab + 5b − 3b − 3 − 12 = **8a − 2ab + 2b − 15**.

**Common mistake:** writing −(2x − 7) as −2x − 7. It must be −2x **+** 7.

**Removing brackets first**: 3(a − b) + 2a = 3a − 3b + 2a = 5a − 3b.

check.q: Subtract 3x − 5 from 7x + 2.

sections.h: Finding the value of an expression
sections.md:
To find the value, **substitute** the given numbers for the variables and calculate (follow BODMAS).

- x + 4 at x = 3 → **7**
- 4x − 3 at x = −1 → −4 − 3 = **−7**
- x² + 2x + 1 at x = 2 → 4 + 4 + 1 = **9**
- a² + 2ab + b² at a = 2, b = −3 → 4 − 12 + 9 = **1**
- 3x² − 2x + 5 at x = 0 → **5**

**Simplify first**, then substitute — faster, with fewer mistakes:
- 2(a² + ab) + 3 − ab at a = 5, b = −3 → 2a² + ab + 3 → 50 − 15 + 3 = **38**.

**Finding an unknown constant**: if 2x² + x − a = 5 when x = 0, then −a = 5 → **a = −5**.

**Watch out with negatives**: (−2)² = 4 but −2² = −4. Always put a substituted negative number in brackets.

check.q: Find the value of 5 − 3x² when x = −2.

sections.h: Using algebraic expressions — formulas and rules
sections.md:
Expressions let us write **general rules** in a short, exact way.

**1. Perimeter formulas**
- Equilateral triangle with side l: P = **3l**
- Square with side l: P = **4l**
- Regular pentagon: **5l**; regular hexagon: **6l**
- Rectangle: **2(l + b)**

**2. Area formulas**
- Square: **l²**; rectangle: **lb**; triangle: **½bh**

Once you have the formula, substitute: a square of side 6.5 cm has area 6.5² = **42.25 cm²**.

**3. Rules for number patterns**
- The nth multiple of 9: **9n**. The 25th is 225.
- The nth even number: **2n**; the nth odd number: **2n − 1**.
- A number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5: **5n + 3**.
- Successor of n: **n + 1**; predecessor: **n − 1**.
- Sum of the first n natural numbers = **n(n + 1)/2** (for n = 10 → 55).

**4. Patterns in geometry**
- Diagonals from **one vertex** of an n-sided polygon: **n − 3**. (Hexagon: 3.)
- Matchstick rows: squares **3n + 1**, triangles **2n + 1**; separate letters L use **2n**, C use **3n**, F use **4n** (count sticks for one letter, multiply by n).

**Did you know?** The word *algebra* comes from the Arabic *al-jabr* in the title of a 9th-century book by al-Khwarizmi. Indian mathematicians like Brahmagupta had earlier used abbreviations (like *yā* for an unknown) to write equations.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch10-algebraic-expres.title: Algebraic Expressions (part 2)
rd-school-c7-maths.ch10-algebraic-expres.subtitle: Tree diagrams, number-pattern rules, the 'nth term', and turning words into expressions.

sections.h: Tree diagrams: seeing the structure of an expression
sections.md:
Take 4x²y − 3xy + 7. Draw it like a family tree:

- **Expression** at the top: 4x²y − 3xy + 7
- Its **terms** on the next level: 4x²y, −3xy, 7
- Each term split into **factors**: 4 × x × x × y; −3 × x × y; 7

The **numerical factor** is the **coefficient**: 4, −3. In −3xy, the coefficient of xy is −3, but you can also say the coefficient of x is −3y. A term with no variable (7) is the **constant term**.

**Writing expressions from words.**
- 5 added to three times y → 3y + 5
- product of p and q, minus 2 → pq − 2
- half of the sum of a and b → (a + b)/2
- the square of m subtracted from 10 → 10 − m²
- one-fourth of z, increased by 6 → z/4 + 6

Read the phrase carefully: 'subtract 4 from x' is x − 4, not 4 − x.

check.q: '7 subtracted from twice n' is—
check.why: Start with twice n, which is 2n, and then take 7 away from it, giving 2n − 7.

sections.h: Number patterns and the nth term
sections.md:
Algebra lets one short rule describe an endless pattern.

- Natural numbers 1, 2, 3, … → nth term **n**
- Even numbers 2, 4, 6, … → **2n**
- Odd numbers 1, 3, 5, … → **2n − 1**
- Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15 … → **5n**
- 3, 7, 11, 15, … (add 4 each time) → **4n − 1**
- Squares 1, 4, 9, 16 … → **n²**

**How to find the rule** for a pattern that grows by the same amount d each time: nth term = d × n + (first term − d). For 3, 7, 11 … d = 4, first term 3 → 4n + (3 − 4) = 4n − 1. Check n = 3: 12 − 1 = 11 ✔.

The 100th odd number is 2(100) − 1 = 199 — no need to list them all!

check.q: The nth term of 6, 11, 16, 21, … is—
check.why: The pattern grows by 5 each time and the first term is 6, so the rule is 5n + (6 − 5) = 5n + 1.

sections.h: Patterns in geometry and other exercise types
sections.md:
**Matchstick and dot shapes.** A row of n squares made of matchsticks needs 3n + 1 sticks. A row of n triangles needs 2n + 1. A pattern of letter L shapes with 2 sticks each uses 2n.

**Diagonals of a polygon.** From one vertex of an n-sided polygon you can draw n − 3 diagonals: a pentagon (5) has 2; a hexagon (6) has 3.

**Perimeter formulas** written as expressions: square 4l, rectangle 2(l + b), equilateral triangle 3l, regular pentagon 5l.

**Exercise types in the chapter:** write expressions from statements; identify terms, factors and coefficients (with tree diagrams); classify as monomial, binomial, trinomial; pick like terms; add and subtract expressions (including 'subtract a from b' order); simplify by combining like terms; find the value for given x, y; find the value of a constant when the expression's value is given (e.g. if x = 0 makes 2x² + x − a equal 5, then a = −5); write rules for patterns.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch11-exponents-powers.title: Exponents and Powers
rd-school-c7-maths.ch11-exponents-powers.subtitle: From grains on a chessboard to the distance to the Sun: powers, the laws of exponents and standard form.

sections.md:
A legend often told in India: a wise man invents chess, and the delighted king offers any reward. The man asks for 1 grain of rice on the first square, 2 on the second, 4 on the third, doubling each time for all 64 squares. The king laughs at such a small request — until his treasurers calculate. The 64th square alone needs 2⁶³ grains: about 9 223 372 036 854 775 808 — more rice than the world has ever grown!

Numbers like that are impossible to read in long form. Some real ones:
- Mass of the Earth ≈ 5 970 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 kg
- Distance from Earth to the Sun ≈ 149 600 000 000 m
- Age of the universe ≈ 13 800 000 000 years

We need a short way to write them. That's what **exponents** do: 10 000 = 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = **10⁴**.

check.q: How many grains are on the 5th square of the chessboard (1, 2, 4, …)?
check.why: Square n has 2^(n−1) grains, so the 5th square has 2⁴ = 16 grains.

sections.md:
> **aⁿ = a × a × a × … × a (n times)**

- **a** is the **base**, **n** is the **exponent** (or index, or power).
- 10⁴ is read '10 raised to the power 4' or 'the fourth power of 10'.
- a² is '**a squared**', a³ is '**a cubed**'.
- 10⁴ is called the **exponential form** of 10 000.

**Powers of 10**: 10 = 10¹, 100 = 10², 1000 = 10³, 1 lakh = 10⁵, 10 lakh = 10⁶, 1 crore = 10⁷.

**Other bases**: 81 = 3⁴; 32 = 2⁵; 125 = 5³; 1000 = 2³ × 5³.

**Variables as base**: a × a × a × b × b = **a³b²**; 2 × 2 × a × a = **2²a²** = 4a².

**Prime factorisation in exponential form**:
- 432 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 = **2⁴ × 3³**
- 3600 = **2⁴ × 3² × 5²**

**Negative bases**
- (−1)¹ = −1, (−1)² = 1, (−1)³ = −1, (−1)⁴ = 1.
- **(−1)^odd = −1** and **(−1)^even = 1**.
- (−2)³ = −8; (−3)⁴ = 81.

**Comparing**: Which is greater, 2³ or 3²? 8 vs 9 → 3². What about 2¹⁰ and 10²? 1024 vs 100 → 2¹⁰ by far!

check.q: Express 729 as a power of 3.
check.why: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 729, which is six factors of 3, so 729 = 3⁶.

sections.md:
**Law 1 — Multiplying powers with the same base: add exponents.**
> aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ

Why? 2³ × 2² = (2 × 2 × 2) × (2 × 2) = 2⁵.
- a⁴ × a¹⁰ = a¹⁴; (−3)² × (−3)³ = (−3)⁵; 5² × 5 × 5⁴ = 5⁷.
- Not for different bases! 2³ × 3² cannot be combined into one power.

**Law 2 — Dividing powers with the same base: subtract exponents.**
> aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (m > n, a ≠ 0)

Why? 3⁷ ÷ 3⁴ = (3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3)/(3 × 3 × 3 × 3) = 3³.
- 7¹⁰ ÷ 7⁸ = 7² = 49; a¹⁵ ÷ a¹⁰ = a⁵.

**Law 3 — Power of a power: multiply exponents.**
> (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ

Why? (2²)³ = 2² × 2² × 2² = 2⁶.
- (5³)² = 5⁶; (a²)⁵ = a¹⁰.
- Which is bigger, 5² × 3 or (5²)³? 75 vs 5⁶ = 15 625.

check.q: Simplify (2³)⁴ ÷ 2⁵.
check.why: (2³)⁴ = 2¹², and dividing by 2⁵ subtracts exponents: 2¹²⁻⁵ = 2⁷.

sections.h: Laws of exponents (2): same exponent, and zero exponent
sections.md:
**Law 4 — Multiplying powers with the same exponent: multiply the bases.**
> aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ

2³ × 3³ = (2 × 2 × 2)(3 × 3 × 3) = (2 × 3)³ = 6³ = 216.
- 4⁴ × 5⁴ = 20⁴; a³ × b³ = (ab)³; (−2)² × 3² = (−6)² = 36.

**Law 5 — Dividing powers with the same exponent: divide the bases.**
> aᵐ ÷ bᵐ = (a/b)ᵐ (b ≠ 0)

- 6⁴ ÷ 3⁴ = 2⁴ = 16; (a/b)⁵ = a⁵/b⁵; (−3)³ ÷ 4³ = (−3/4)³ = −27/64.

**Law 6 — Zero exponent.**
> a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0)

Why? 3⁴ ÷ 3⁴ = 1 (anything divided by itself), and by Law 2 it is 3⁴⁻⁴ = 3⁰. So 3⁰ = 1.
- 7⁰ = 1; (−25)⁰ = 1; (2/3)⁰ = 1; 1000⁰ = 1.
- But 2 × 3⁰ = 2 × 1 = 2, while (2 × 3)⁰ = 1.

| Law | Rule |
|---|---|
| 1 | aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ |
| 2 | aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ |
| 3 | (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ |
| 4 | aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ |
| 5 | aᵐ ÷ bᵐ = (a/b)ᵐ |
| 6 | a⁰ = 1 |

check.q: What is the value of (3⁰ + 2⁰) × 5⁰?
check.why: Each power with exponent 0 equals 1, so (1 + 1) × 1 = 2.

sections.md:
The trick is to **write everything with prime bases**, then apply the laws.

**Example 1.** (2⁵ × 2³) ÷ 2⁶ = 2⁸ ÷ 2⁶ = 2² = **4**.

**Example 2.** (3⁴ × 9²) ÷ 27². Write 9 = 3² and 27 = 3³:
- (3⁴ × 3⁴) ÷ 3⁶ = 3⁸ ÷ 3⁶ = 3² = **9**.

**Example 3.** (25 × 5² × t⁸) ÷ (10³ × t⁴).
- 25 × 5² = 5⁴; 10³ = 2³ × 5³.
- = 5⁴t⁸ / (2³ × 5³ × t⁴) = **(5/8)t⁴**.

**Example 4.** (2⁵ × 3² × 7) ÷ (8 × 3 × 7) = 2⁵ × 3² × 7 / (2³ × 3 × 7) = 2² × 3 = **12**.

**Example 5.** Find m if 2ᵐ × 2³ = 2⁸ → m + 3 = 8 → **m = 5**.

**Example 6.** Is 2⁴ = 4²? 16 = 16 ✔ — a rare coincidence. But 2³ ≠ 3² (8 ≠ 9).

**True or false?**
- 10 × 10¹¹ = 100¹¹ ✘ (it is 10¹²).
- 2³ > 5² ✘ (8 < 25).
- 2³ × 3² = 6⁵ ✘ (bases and exponents both differ).
- 3⁰ = 1000⁰ ✔ (both are 1).

check.q: Simplify (4³ × 2²) ÷ 2⁵.
check.why: 4³ = 2⁶, so the numerator is 2⁶ × 2² = 2⁸, and 2⁸ ÷ 2⁵ = 2³ = 8.

sections.h: Decimal number system and powers of 10
sections.md:
Our place-value system is built on powers of 10. In **expanded form**:

> 47 561 = 4 × 10 000 + 7 × 1000 + 5 × 100 + 6 × 10 + 1
> = **4 × 10⁴ + 7 × 10³ + 5 × 10² + 6 × 10¹ + 1 × 10⁰**

The exponent of 10 for each digit equals the number of places to its right.

- 172 = 1 × 10² + 7 × 10¹ + 2 × 10⁰
- 5643 = 5 × 10³ + 6 × 10² + 4 × 10¹ + 3 × 10⁰
- 70 004 = 7 × 10⁴ + 4 × 10⁰
- 1 03 278 = 1 × 10⁵ + 3 × 10³ + 2 × 10² + 7 × 10¹ + 8 × 10⁰

**Did you know?** The decimal place-value system with zero was developed in India (it appears in sources such as the Bakhshali manuscript and the works of Aryabhata and Brahmagupta), travelled through the Arab world, and reached Europe as 'Hindu-Arabic numerals'.

check.q: Which number is 3 × 10⁴ + 2 × 10² + 5 × 10⁰?
check.why: 3 ten-thousands, 0 thousands, 2 hundreds, 0 tens and 5 ones make 30 205.

sections.h: Expressing large numbers in standard form
sections.md:
**Standard form** (scientific notation): write a number as
> **k × 10ⁿ**, where **1 ≤ k < 10** and n is a whole number.

Steps: put the decimal point after the **first non-zero digit**, then count how many places it moved — that's n.

- 5985 = 5.985 × 10³
- 3 430 000 = 3.43 × 10⁶
- Speed of light ≈ 300 000 000 m/s = **3 × 10⁸ m/s**
- Earth–Sun distance ≈ 149 600 000 000 m = **1.496 × 10¹¹ m**
- Diameter of the Earth ≈ 12 756 000 m = **1.2756 × 10⁷ m**
- Population of India ≈ 1 400 000 000 = **1.4 × 10⁹** (approximate)
- 40.43 × 10⁷ is **not** standard form (40.43 ≥ 10) → = 4.043 × 10⁸.

**Comparing large numbers is easy in standard form**: the larger power of 10 wins first. Moon ≈ 3.84 × 10⁸ m away, Sun ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m → the Sun is roughly 400 times farther.

**Zeros check**: 10ⁿ has n zeros. So 10⁹ = one billion = 100 crore.

**Adding in standard form** — make exponents the same: 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg (Earth) + 7.35 × 10²² kg (Moon) = 597 × 10²² + 7.35 × 10²² = 604.35 × 10²² = **6.0435 × 10²⁴ kg**.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch11-exponents-powers.title: Exponents and Powers (part 2)
rd-school-c7-maths.ch11-exponents-powers.subtitle: Negative bases, prime-factor powers, comparing giant numbers and space-sized standard form.

sections.h: Negative bases and the sign rule
sections.md:
(−1)¹ = −1, (−1)² = +1, (−1)³ = −1, (−1)⁴ = +1 …

> A negative number raised to an **even** power is **positive**; raised to an **odd** power it is **negative**.

- (−2)³ = (−2)(−2)(−2) = −8
- (−3)⁴ = 81
- (−1)¹⁰¹ = −1, (−1)¹⁰⁰⁰ = 1

**Careful:** −3² means −(3²) = −9, but (−3)² = 9. Brackets matter!

**Powers of fractions:** (2/3)³ = 2³/3³ = 8/27; (−1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

check.q: (−5)³ equals—
check.why: An odd power of a negative number is negative, and 5³ = 125, so (−5)³ = −125.

sections.h: Writing numbers as products of prime powers
sections.md:
Any whole number can be written using powers of its prime factors.

- 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = **2³ × 3²**
- 432 = 2⁴ × 3³ (16 × 27 = 432 ✔)
- 1000 = 2³ × 5³ = 10³
- 16000 = 2⁷ × 5³ (128 × 125 = 16000 ✔)

**Expressing as a power of one base:** 729 = 3⁶; 1024 = 2¹⁰; 64 = 2⁶ = 4³ = 8².

**Comparing powers.** Which is greater, 2⁸ or 8²? 2⁸ = 256, 8² = 64 → 2⁸. Which is greater, 3⁴ or 4³? 81 vs 64 → 3⁴. Exponents grow numbers far faster than multiplication: 10⁵ is a lakh, 10⁷ a crore.

**Power of a power:** (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, e.g. (2³)² = 2⁶ = 64. **Product with same exponent:** aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ, e.g. 2³ × 5³ = 10³.

check.q: Which is larger: 2¹⁰ or 10²?
check.why: 2¹⁰ = 1024 while 10² = 100, so 2¹⁰ is much larger.

sections.h: Standard form in science, and exercise types
sections.md:
Standard form is k × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ k < 10.

| Quantity | Standard form |
|---|---|
| Distance Earth–Sun ≈ 149,600,000 km | 1.496 × 10⁸ km |
| Speed of light ≈ 300,000,000 m/s | 3 × 10⁸ m/s |
| Population of India ≈ 1.4 billion | 1.4 × 10⁹ |
| Mass of Earth ≈ 5,970,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg | 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg |

To write 4,30,000 in standard form, move the decimal 5 places left: **4.3 × 10⁵**. To expand 7.02 × 10⁶: 7,020,000.

**Expanded form with powers of 10:** 47561 = 4 × 10⁴ + 7 × 10³ + 5 × 10² + 6 × 10 + 1 × 10⁰.

**Exercise types:** find the value (2⁶, 9³); write in exponential form; express as prime powers; compare pairs; simplify with the laws (e.g. (3⁷ ÷ 3⁵)⁴ = 3⁸); say true/false for statements like 10 × 10¹¹ = 100¹¹ (false: it is 10¹²); write in expanded form; convert to and from standard form.

Express 540 as a product of prime powers.
Write 0.5 × 10⁷ correctly in standard form.
steps: k must be between 1 and 10: 0.5 = 5 × 10⁻¹... instead shift: 0.5 × 10⁷ = 5,000,000.

rd-school-c7-maths.ch12-symmetry.title: Symmetry
rd-school-c7-maths.ch12-symmetry.subtitle: Rangoli, butterflies and spinning wheels: mirror lines and turning shapes

sections.md:
On Diwali morning, Ananya's grandmother draws a rangoli at the doorstep. She draws one petal, then repeats it, turning and reflecting, until a perfect flower blooms. Whichever way you look at it, the pattern seems balanced. That balance has a mathematical name: **symmetry**.

Symmetry is everywhere: in the Taj Mahal's front view, in a peepal leaf, in the Ashoka Chakra, in snowflakes and starfish, in company logos and in the wheels of a bullock cart. Artists, architects, textile designers and engineers use it constantly because symmetric shapes feel pleasing and are often strong and balanced. A bridge with two equal halves shares its load evenly; a car wheel with equal spokes spins without wobbling.

The chapter moves in this order:
1. **Introduction** and a quick revision of line symmetry from Class 6.
2. **Lines of symmetry for regular polygons.**
3. **Rotational symmetry** — centre, angle and order of rotation.
4. **Line symmetry and rotational symmetry** together — which shapes have one, both or neither.

Along the way you will do paper-folding, ink-blot and paper-cutting activities, complete half-drawn figures on squared paper, and spin cut-out shapes to count how often they match themselves.

check.q: Which of these is the best everyday example of symmetry?
options: A random ink blot spread unevenly
The front view of the Taj Mahal
check.why: The Taj Mahal's front view has a vertical line that splits it into two mirror-image halves.

sections.md:
A figure has **line symmetry** if a line can be drawn through it so that one half is the **mirror image** of the other. Fold along that line and the halves cover each other exactly. The line is the **line (axis) of symmetry**.

**Two ways to test a line:**
- **Fold test:** trace the figure, fold along the line; if the two parts overlap exactly, it is a line of symmetry.
- **Mirror test:** stand a small mirror on the line. If the reflection plus the visible half makes the whole figure again, the line is a line of symmetry.

**Mirror reflection and symmetry are closely linked.** When you look in a mirror, your image is as far behind the mirror as you are in front, and left and right appear swapped. Every point of one half of a symmetric figure has a partner point on the other half: the same distance from the line, on a perpendicular to the line. That is exactly what a mirror does.

A shape can have **no**, **one**, **two** or **many** lines of symmetry:

| Figure | Lines of symmetry |
|---|---|
| Scalene triangle | 0 |
| Isosceles triangle | 1 |
| Kite | 1 |
| Rectangle | 2 |
| Rhombus | 2 (its diagonals) |
| Equilateral triangle | 3 |
| Square | 4 |
| Parallelogram (not a rectangle or rhombus) | 0 |
| Semicircle | 1 |
| Circle | infinitely many (every diameter) |

Careful: a rectangle's **diagonals are not** lines of symmetry. Fold a rectangular paper along a diagonal and the corners do not match. In a square, however, they are.

keyTerms: Line of symmetry — a fold line that makes two halves match exactly
Mirror image — the reflected copy, same size, left and right swapped

check.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
check.why: A square has 2 lines through midpoints of opposite sides and 2 along its diagonals, 4 in all.

sections.h: Making symmetric figures: ink blots, paper cuts and squared paper
sections.md:
**Ink-blot activity.** Fold a sheet in half, open it, and drop a few blobs of ink or paint near the fold on one side. Press the halves together and open. The blot has spread into a figure that is symmetric about the fold. Try two colours and you get a mirror-image butterfly.

**Paper-cutting activity.** Fold a square sheet in half and cut a design along the folded edge; when you open it, the design has one line of symmetry. Fold it twice (into quarters) before cutting and you get two lines of symmetry. Fold a square along both diagonals too (eighths) and the opened cut-out has four lines of symmetry — this is how paper snowflakes and Sanjhi stencils are made.

**Completing a figure on squared paper.** You are given half a figure and a dotted mirror line. To complete it:
1. Pick a corner point of the given half.
2. Count how many squares it is from the mirror line (along a line perpendicular to the mirror).
3. Mark a point the **same number of squares** on the other side.
4. Do this for every corner and join the points in the same order.

If the mirror line is slanting (diagonal of the squares), count diagonally: a point 2 squares right and 1 square up of the line goes 1 right and 2 up... the easiest method is to fold the squared paper along the diagonal and prick through the corners.

**Figures with two mirror lines.** If two perpendicular mirror lines are given, reflect the given part in one line first, then reflect both parts in the second line. You end up with four copies, like a rangoli quadrant repeated.

> Did you know? Many Indian textile prints — Ajrakh from Kutch, Kalamkari borders, Kanchipuram sari motifs — are built by reflecting one small block again and again.

check.q: A square sheet is folded into quarters (two perpendicular folds) and a design is cut. How many lines of symmetry will the opened design surely have?
check.why: Each fold becomes a mirror line, so two perpendicular folds give at least two lines of symmetry.

sections.h: Lines of symmetry for regular polygons
sections.md:
A **polygon** is a closed figure made of line segments. It is **regular** when all its sides are equal **and** all its angles are equal. An equilateral triangle is the regular polygon of 3 sides; a square is the regular polygon of 4 sides; then come the regular pentagon (5), hexagon (6), heptagon (7), octagon (8), and so on.

The key fact of this section:

**A regular polygon with n sides has exactly n lines of symmetry.**

| Regular polygon | Sides | Lines of symmetry |
|---|---|---|
| Equilateral triangle | 3 | 3 |
| Square | 4 | 4 |
| Regular pentagon | 5 | 5 |
| Regular hexagon | 6 | 6 |
| Regular octagon | 8 | 8 |
| Regular decagon | 10 | 10 |

**Where do the lines go?**
- If n is **odd** (triangle, pentagon), every line goes from a corner (vertex) to the midpoint of the opposite side.
- If n is **even** (square, hexagon), half the lines join opposite corners and half join midpoints of opposite sides.

As n grows, the polygon looks more and more like a circle, which has infinitely many lines of symmetry.

**Irregular shapes** need not follow any rule. A rectangle has 4 sides but only 2 lines; a general quadrilateral may have none. Being regular is what guarantees n lines.

**Letters of the English alphabet** (simple block capitals):
- Vertical line: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y
- Horizontal line: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X
- Both: H, I, O, X
- None: F, G, J, L, N, P, Q, R, S, Z

Natural objects and human-made objects also show line symmetry: leaves, a human face (roughly), a kite, the Gateway of India, the national emblem.

fig.alt: Regular pentagon and hexagon with their lines of symmetry

check.q: A regular octagon has how many lines of symmetry?
check.why: A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry, so a regular octagon has 8.

sections.md:
Spin a ceiling fan with three blades. Before it completes a full turn, it looks exactly the same **three** times: after 120°, 240° and 360°. This is **rotational symmetry**: a figure looks exactly the same after being turned about a point through some angle less than a full turn.

Vocabulary:
- **Centre of rotation**: the fixed point about which the shape turns. For regular polygons, rectangles, parallelograms and circles it is the point where the diagonals (or lines of symmetry) meet; for a circle, its centre.
- **Angle of rotation**: the smallest angle turned for the shape to look the same again.
- **Order of rotational symmetry**: the number of times the shape looks exactly the same in one full turn (360°).

Angle of rotation = 360° ÷ order, and order = 360° ÷ angle.

**Words for turns:** a **quarter turn** = 90°, a **half turn** = 180°, a **three-quarter turn** = 270°, a **full turn** = 360°. Rotations may be **clockwise** (like clock hands) or **anticlockwise**; the order does not depend on the direction.

**Activity — the tracing test.** Trace a shape on tracing paper, pin it at the centre with a pencil tip, and slowly turn it. Count how many times the tracing sits exactly on the shape before returning to the start. Marking one corner with a dot helps you know when a full turn is complete.

| Shape | Order | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| Square | 4 | 90° |
| Equilateral triangle | 3 | 120° |
| Rectangle | 2 | 180° |
| Regular pentagon | 5 | 72° |
| Regular hexagon | 6 | 60° |
| Circle | infinite | any angle |
| Letter S, Z, N | 2 | 180° |
| Windmill with 4 equal blades | 4 | 90° |

Every shape returns to itself after 360°, so we say a shape has rotational symmetry only if its order is **more than 1**. A shape of order 1 (like an isosceles triangle, a kite or the letter F) has **no** rotational symmetry.

The centre of rotation need not be inside the shape's coloured part: for a ring-shaped design, the centre is in the empty middle.
